# Top 5 posts from r/MovieSuggestions day

## 1. Looking for more recent “so bad they’re good” movies that aren’t trying to be.

**Score:** 72
**Body:** Please no Sharknado, no Birdemic, no VelociPastor. That’s great if you like those type of  movies, but they just don’t do it for me. I can tell they were trying to be bad on purpose. I need to be able to tell whoever was behind making the movie thought they were making something great but failed. 

The most obvious to me is The Room but EVERYONE has seen that. You can tell he thought he was killin’ it. Some other examples would be LOL, Dear Evan Hansen, Twilight, The Kissing Booth. 

Please and thank you. 

### Top 10 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. Cats probably didn't turn out quite as well as everyone involved seemed to think it would.
2. Megalopolis
3. Moonfall is always my go to and my favourite dreadful movie 
4. Serenity

# Top 5 posts from r/TrueFilm day

## 1. "The Odyssey" is far from the visual treat I was expecting

**Score:** 347
**Body:** I finally watched “The Odyssey” as “Nolan intended” - there are few IMAX screens near me and pre-ticket sales for those showings were insane - but, while I was watching it, all I could think of was this did not look like the work of a confident director, but of someone that’s (way too) confident in his 'directorial brand'.

It's like Nolan KNOWS that we KNOW about his CGI-aversion (or was trusting we’d get the message from the A-list cast members who won’t shut up about it). So he storyboarded a film that looks more impressive when we’re removed from it than when we're absorbed by it. The shots at sea, for instance, are screaming for the audience to be in awe of the technical difficulties; he wanted us to think "wow, Matt Damon really had to earn his millions in this one".

But other than a couple of standout sequences – namely, the superbly staged act featuring Samantha Morton as Circe –, the movie itself is visually unremarkable and below Nolan’s standards. The visual symmetry of “Dunkirk”, a film that I respect but not quite like, is gone. The battle scenes are generically choreographed, and the mise en scène was lacking even in crucial interior shots, including the climax. (Did Matt Damon kill Mia Goth or is she still hiding under the table?? And don't get me started on Tom Holland's knife fight upstairs.)

Sadly, it seems the difficulty came at the expense of the execution, which is not nearly as refined as in his previous movies - even the editing pace, which was very "on brand" for a Nolan release, gave me the feeling of a director trying to save some subpar takes here and there. I won't go over the shortcomings of the script, which is in line with what I came to expect from Nolan as a blockbuster maker.

But I'll mention one element of the picture that clearly stands out: the elegance and precision of Ludwig Göransson's score, which Nolan's directorial achievement never quite matches. He can do better, and has done better.

### Top 2 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. I liked his rendition of the monsters (cyclops, Circe, the cliffside monster etc) and his reimagined character arc for Odysseus. Some other scenes like the massive storm near the end are impactful especially on a big screen, partly thanks to sheer LOUDNESS but also the practical effects. 

I do agree that the final brawl against the suitors is not very well choreographed or interesting, which was disappointing. 

I probably enjoyed this most of all Nolan films I've seen, partly because some of his quirks (heavy-handed dialogue for instance) don't feel entirely out of place in a grand myth, and partly because his strengths worked well in this context
  - Nolan’s heavy handed dialogue was probably the most noticeably out of place element of the film. To go from the language of the poem, no matter the translation, to what was on screen, was baffling. 
    - Agreed. Dialogue was the weakest part of the film. I don't understand the hype for this film tbh. Not saying it wasn't good, it's a good film to watch in the theater. I just don't think it's this unbelievable masterpiece. Nolan almost feels like more of a technician than an auteur at times. However the actors seem to love him so who am I to judge.
      - I didn't like the film very much but the hype is easy to understand: big, expensive film from a very popular director (Nolan has mass appeal, despite what we think) based on a story that almost every westerner has at the very least heard of, featuring a ton of big name actors and cool technical sequences. People that don't normally dissect films are seeing this movie and raving about it to their friends, and that plus the huge maketing budget means that this movie is going to earn billions over its lifetime.
    - Sometimes true, but I guess my reading was that ancient myths aren't always exactly subtle about exposition either lol so it didn't necessarily feel untrue to the *spirit* of a grand myth.
      - Homer's dialogue definitely isn't subtle, but the language of the poem is stunningly beautiful. The descriptions are incredibly vivid and the metaphors are really striking. There's a reason it has held up for 2700 years. 

I think it's also part of the reason why it's so hard to adapt the poem into a movie. The language itself is a huge part of why the poem is so good and one of the recurring themes of the poem is the power of using the right words in the right situation.
        - I somehow agree with both of you. The exposition doesn’t necessarily hurt the dialogue when we are watching an epic movie. But then it also needs to be handled in a particular way to be palatable and elevated. In this particular movie, the heavy handed dialogue made the exposition so distilled and dumbed down that the “epic grandeur” relied solely on visuals and plot points (which sometimes delivered but not always).
  - The final brawl against the suitors was basically a marginally improved re-do of the end of The Dark Knight Rises when the army of unarmed Gotham police charges the army of Bane mercenaries with rifles and they all proceed to have a giant fistfight. 

There are no dramatic stakes, the action itself is either dancey and weightless or weirdly sloppy, it goes on for way too long, and there's no real sense of what's actually *happening* beyond CHAOS CHAOS CHAOS. In both cases, I found myself ready for the scene to be over about five minutes before it actually ended. 

Plus, having taught the Homeric version in a high school setting many times, it was a bummer to see the entire scene transformed from the original "Odysseus annihilates every single suitor (plus a bunch of his own servants who were coerced into 'disloyalty')" into "Odysseus fights the bad suitors." I understand that the latter is far more acceptable by modern sensibilities, but Homer's Odysseus vs the suitors is less a fight and more like the Ark of the Covenant vs the Nazis.
    - I don’t even remember that Dark Knight Rises scene….which kinda proves the point you’re making haha
  - Poorly choreographed fight scenes are Nolan trademark at this point

## 2. Rewatched 'Under the Skin' and legitimately think it might be my current favorite film

**Score:** 89
**Body:** I first tried watching this film back when I was maybe 17 and had just recently started getting into less overtly commercial films, but I was watching it on a laptop with earbuds (lol) and maybe made it 20 minutes before I found myself unable to stay awake. 

A few years ago, though, A24 re-released a few of their films with this being one of them, and considering I hadn't seen it properly before, I figured I would be able to appreciate it now that I was much more steeped in weirder, less accessible material.

Not only did it completely land for me, but after rewatching it just a few days ago, I honestly think it's one of the most raw, primal examples of what the entire medium of film is capable of. I also picked up on a lot more this time; the backgrounds of the aliens environments are literally depicted as being completely black and completely white. The aliens exist in a world of hyper, stark objectivity, where there is no sense of value to life, just the consumption of it.

With the obvious implication that a woman walking alone will inevitably be subject to predation, and with the sensitivity of her skin being the sole thing keeping her from being found out, the entire plan revolves around her flipping the script on its head, by traveling protected in a large cargo van. One sequence finds her suddenly surrounded by a group of hooligans banging against the vehicle, and she looks at them so distantly it's like she doesn't even perceive that they're trying to be threatening.

However, the turning point in the film comes after witnessing the incident with the surfer and the family, the first time we ever see or hear her actually being made aware of the result of her refusal to help someone. She listens to a radio broadcast detailing the missing victims, and soon after, finds herself driving into a wall full of mist.

Originally, this scene confused me: I did wonder why she would choose to get out of the van and abandon her sense of protection in order to move forward on foot, rather than just turning around or waiting for the mist to clear. However, on a rewatch, it became abundantly clear to me what the real meaning of this scene was: for a creature whose entire existence is black and white, the discovery of actual nuance and subjectivity leaves them, for the first time, in a literal 'gray area'. 

I also noticed another interesting theme, which is the way that all four elements play a very distinct role in the aliens experience:

Earth - The first moment where the alien is taken out of its sense of control is when it trips and falls on the ground, dazed and frightened by the unfamiliar experience. Later, with the one man who chooses to be kind, the alien finds itself petrified to the point of needing to be slowly walked down the steps one at a time, facing the concept of legitimate mortality with no preparation.  

Water - The surfer and the family on the beach being swept away serving as the ultimate proof of the film that it is not human, by depicting a sequence so upsetting that any conscious able-bodied human would find themselves biologically compelled to intervene

Air - The wall of mist representing the aliens ultimate seduction into trying to be human after discovering the feelings associated with nuance and subjectivity. 

Fire - The attacker in the woods, finding out the truth and seeing the aliens true form, chooses to set it alight, the 'baptism/cleansing by flame' serving as the punishment for the sin of pretending to be human. As the flames burn out, only the ashes of the true form remain. 

We slowly fade away into a calming image of falling snow with the familiar sound of crackling fire, only to abruptly be thrust into the films credits, the unnerving score immediately extinguishing the first brief glimpse of comfort or warmth the film has had to offer. A truly, definitively alien experience. 

### Top 6 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. I haven't seen it in years but, yeah, this has always been a favorite of mine. Nice writeup. I've always been enamored with the idea of gender in the film. At around the flip point (scene on the beach) you see the alien becoming, or at least wanting to become, a woman - everything preceding that was just cosplay (for lack of a better word). To pair it with your analysis, it's like gender itself can't exist in this purely objective state but only arises out of subjectivity. The scene where she's looking at her body in the mirror and Mica Levi's track "Love" plays is one of my favorite scenes of the film.
2. Maybe my favorite movie as well. I think on a first watch it can come across as thin, pretentious, or just boring, but it really rewards repeat viewings. It's a very carefully made film. Every moment advances the story and themes. It's also just a gorgeous movie, both visually and aurally.
3. It's a great film and in my opinion Glazer's best so far. 

I really like your observation about the four elements in the film. Its power, I think, lies in the way it works like some kind of classical myth. The main character's journey feels monumental somehow, epic. The idea of her passing through earth, water, air, and fire fits well. 

This might be a bit out there, but I wonder if there's an argument to be made that Under The Skin works as a Christian film. On one level it's a story about an alien experiencing a kind of universal humanity, like Arrival in reverse. Even if that's a ridiculous interpretation, it's undeniable there are spiritual themes in the film. 

Something that puzzles me about Glazer is how he was able to tell a story about aliens with such a deep sense of humanity, and yet his portrayal of nazis was so entirely alien.
4. It's so creepy and atmospheric and awesome. Also, it doesn't get talked about but scarlet johansen's accent in that movie was pretty great. I don't know, I'm not Scottish, but it sounded spot on to me
5. It is one of my favorite films on many levels.

The otherworldliness and alien feeling of Scotland, the predation script inverted then recalled, the haunting music, the alien "discovering" their own vulnerability and interconnectedness to others despite their disconnection to their apparent form, the reliance on visual storytelling, and the reluctance to spell things out with obvious expository dialog are all exceptional.

Regarding the elements, that is an interesting take.

One thing I would note that the original post leaves out, is that the tower with the steps is reminiscent of the path down into the darkness, and ultimately doom, of the victims into the black pool. The alien's fear may be due to a recognition of that similarity.

## 4. anyone fond of Hal Hartley's works?

**Score:** 30
**Body:** I just saw his film "Meanwhile" which was my 9th film of his filmography and I gotta say he's spot on 9 for 9 thus far.  It's actually incredible stuff, I've never encountered a more consistent filmography. Every single film has a stark script that's both sardonic, sincere at the same time. I'm curious why he didn't end up receiving the same fame as his other contemporary indie filmmakers like Jarmusch or Tarantino. His style is one of a kind.

### Top 6 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. Hartley is an underrated director. The guy was onto something very different. Genuinely surprised that some of his 80s and 90s films have fallen out of print. Unbelievable Truth and Trust could be / should be Criterion releases with bonus content. 
2. Huge fan to the point that I made a thesis on him :)  
Unbelievable Truth, Trust and Simple Men are masterpieces. Surviving Desire, a "long short film", is a favorite of mine.

But I have to admit that I found Henry Fool icky - the rape of a 13-year old girl is one of the themes - and although the movie is ambigious, I don't think Hartley handled that subject very well. Many love the movie, but had it come out today I think it would have been viewed differently. That is often the case, but I really had a hard time with it back then also.

Another, less dramatic, later change in Hartley's films was when he shifted to digital. I think Michael Spiller's camerawork is not mentioned enough in relation to Hartley's work.
